storySpine.startingBelief: B.Com and BBA are fundamentally different in content.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student is comparing course lists to choose a degree.
storySpine.observation: Both programmes list Business Organization & Management in Semester I.
storySpine.focus: Degree titles do not guarantee subject exclusivity.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: One shared title invalidates the assumption that lists are totally distinct.
storySpine.changedAction: Shift from relying on degree titles to checking specific official documents.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student writes down the exact document title and page number for future verification.
storySpine.channelExperience: A systematic look at official data that corrects a common assumption.

candidates.title: The Shared Title Check
candidates.audienceGap: Belief that degree names define all internal subject matter.
candidates.viewerChange: Understands that specific course documents, not degree titles, define overlap.
candidates.concept: Verification of shared course content in official documents.
candidates.device: Side-by-side display of two official PDF pages.
candidates.payoff: Student stops guessing and references specific, verifiable course documents.
candidates.hlni: Business Organization & Management appears in both JOY University B.Com (p.5) and BBA (p.9) documents for 2025 onwards; source: https://joyuniversity.edu.in/B.Com%20Accounting%20and%20Finance.pdf and https://joyuniversity.edu.in/BBA%20Entrepreneurship%20Management.pdf.
candidates.support: Official JOY University PDF, B.Com Accounting & Finance p.5 and BBA Entrepreneurship Management p.9; covers identify the 2025–26-onwards cohort.
methodSteps: Identify the specific programme and document cohort.
Show the inspected course-title row in each source.
Use this bounded overlap to investigate the full course, rather than assume degree titles partition subjects.
candidates.interpretationRule: The supplied rows establish this shared title in these two documents only; they do not establish identical teaching, depth, assessment or availability.
candidates.visibleProof: Visual highlight of the same row in two separate official documents.
candidates.limitations: No universal overlap, identical content, exclusivity, current-admissions or career inference. BBA later sections are inconsistent; use only the inspected row.

demonstration.input: Two official course documents for B.Com and BBA.
demonstration.observation: The same subject appears in both programme documents.
demonstration.nextQuestion: What other specific subjects actually overlap in these programmes?

storySpine.startingBelief: A subject list is enough to evaluate a course.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student is looking at a prospective programme brochure.
storySpine.observation: The list mentions a project, but lacks criteria for what is evaluated.
storySpine.focus: Distinguishing between the activity and the assessment method.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Knowing the activity doesn't reveal the standard for success.
storySpine.changedAction: Student creates a three-column sheet to list product, criteria, and feedback.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student identifies missing assessment criteria as the key knowledge gap.
storySpine.channelExperience: A clear, rational method for evaluating curriculum depth.

candidates.title: The Assessment Audit
candidates.audienceGap: Assumption that subject names equate to knowing course rigor.
candidates.viewerChange: Learns to ask for assessment criteria rather than just titles.
candidates.payoff: Student prepares to contact the department with specific, informed questions.
candidates.hlni: A task label alone does not disclose the expected work product, assessment criteria, or feedback mechanisms.
candidates.support: Reasoning based on assessment design principles.
methodSteps: Write the expected work product.
Ask what criterion is used to assess it.
Ask what feedback is available; mark unknown answers as questions.
candidates.interpretationRule: Use the unanswered cells to ask a precise question about the actual course or task before deciding.
candidates.visibleProof: The transformation of a blank sheet into a structured inquiry tool.
candidates.limitations: This is a question-forming aid, not a degree ranking, aptitude test or prediction of success.

demonstration.visibleInput: Task: Conduct a market analysis for a local startup.
demonstration.observation: The criteria for evaluating the analysis are not listed.
demonstration.nextQuestion: What specific criteria are used to grade this analysis?

storySpine.startingBelief: I should choose the degree my friend chose to be safe.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student feels anxious about choosing the 'wrong' degree.
storySpine.observation: Both friends try a mock case study but struggle at different points.
storySpine.focus: Identifying personal needs in a task rather than following a friend.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Different sticking points show they value different aspects of the process.
storySpine.changedAction: Student records their own specific question about the task instead of copying their friend's choice.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student initiates a conversation with an advisor about their specific struggle.
storySpine.channelExperience: A relatable, low-pressure exploration of personal academic needs.

candidates.title: The Task Journal
candidates.audienceGap: Choosing a degree based on peer validation rather than individual curiosity.
candidates.viewerChange: Uses task struggles as a signal for investigation rather than a reason for panic.
candidates.concept: Personalized task journaling to uncover individual interests.
candidates.device: Split-screen conversation about a sample task.
candidates.payoff: Student feels confident asking questions relevant to their own learning journey.
candidates.hlni: A short activity reveals where you need help and what to investigate, rather than determining degree fit.
methodSteps: Try or inspect a clearly illustrative task.
Record one point where you needed help and one question you want to investigate.
Turn the observation into a question for a real course brief or course team.
candidates.interpretationRule: Use the recorded observation to choose the next question, not to select a degree from one activity.
candidates.visibleProof: Two friends recording different, specific questions on their respective journals.
candidates.limitations: A brief exercise does not measure aptitude, learning style, long-term interest or academic performance.

demonstration.input: A sample business case study about pricing.
demonstration.visibleInput: Task: Set a price for a new product.
demonstration.observation: I don't know how to factor in fixed costs.
demonstration.nextQuestion: Can you explain the framework for calculating fixed costs?

storySpine.startingBelief: I must decide between B.Com and BBA right now.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student is worried about picking a degree without being 'sure'.
storySpine.observation: The student lists preferences but realizes they don't know the requirements for those choices.
storySpine.focus: Separating personal preference from verified requirement.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Desire doesn't guarantee availability or fit.
storySpine.changedAction: Student moves preferences to a 'to-verify' list with concrete check-boxes.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student feels relieved to have a checklist instead of a final decision.
storySpine.channelExperience: Supportive validation that research is better than guessing.

candidates.title: The Preference Check
candidates.audienceGap: Confusing personal desire with confirmed degree availability/fit.
candidates.viewerChange: Moves from passive worrying to active verification.
candidates.payoff: Student successfully moves from anxiety to an actionable research plan.
candidates.hlni: Preferences are not confirmations; unknown requirements must be checked before a degree choice is treated as valid.
candidates.support: Reasoning based on decision-making under uncertainty.
methodSteps: Name the option you prefer.
List the actual requirements you need to check and mark unknowns.
Verify an unknown before treating the option as available.
candidates.interpretationRule: Use an unknown requirement as the next verification task; preference alone is not confirmation.
candidates.visibleProof: The student ticking off 'verified' items and highlighting 'unknown' items.
candidates.limitations: Never invent eligibility rules, admission availability or prerequisites.

demonstration.input: A list of preferred course features.
demonstration.visibleInput: Preference: I want an internship-focused curriculum.
demonstration.observation: I have not checked if these internships are compulsory or elective.
demonstration.nextQuestion: Where can I find the specific internship requirements for this course?

storySpine.startingBelief: A sample task result is proof of a degree's identity.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student is looking at an unlabeled business assignment.
storySpine.observation: The task could plausibly exist in either B.Com or BBA.
storySpine.focus: Identifying that one example is insufficient to categorize a whole degree.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Absence of link makes exclusive classification impossible.
storySpine.changedAction: Student moves from guessing to identifying the missing source.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student marks the task as 'unlinked' and seeks the official syllabus.
storySpine.channelExperience: A 'detective' style investigation that rewards curiosity.

candidates.title: The Unlabeled Challenge
candidates.audienceGap: Tendency to overgeneralize from a single unverified example.
candidates.viewerChange: Learns to question the source of information rather than assuming it proves a label.
candidates.payoff: Student demonstrates critical thinking by refusing to guess without evidence.
candidates.hlni: One unlabeled example does not prove which degree contains it; an exclusive claim requires a source linking the task to the programme.
methodSteps: Present one example without a source linking it to a category.
Separate a plausible guess from what the available information proves.
Identify the exact missing source or information needed to decide.
candidates.interpretationRule: Answer not enough information when the necessary link is absent, then name the evidence that would resolve it.
candidates.visibleProof: The card 'Not Enough Information' is placed over the B.Com/BBA labels.
candidates.limitations: Do not assert that the example belongs to both degrees, or to either one, without actual curriculum evidence.

demonstration.input: An unlabeled case study about budget management.
demonstration.visibleInput: Task: Prepare a quarterly financial forecast.
demonstration.observation: There is no source document linking this task to a specific degree.
demonstration.nextQuestion: Which specific document confirms where this task is taught?

storySpine.startingBelief: If the totals are the same, the content is the same.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student compares two degree structures based on total credit counts.
storySpine.observation: Two programmes have equal credits but different credit-allocation patterns.
storySpine.focus: Understanding that aggregates hide underlying variations.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Total equality does not imply identical component experience.
storySpine.changedAction: Student breaks down the total into individual components before comparing.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student finds a difference in credit distribution that changes their perspective.
storySpine.channelExperience: A visual 'aha!' moment using simple arithmetic.

candidates.title: The Aggregate Reveal
candidates.audienceGap: Confusing aggregate totals with component-level similarity.
candidates.viewerChange: Learns to look for breakdowns rather than relying on totals.
candidates.payoff: Student discovers that identical totals can conceal different learning paths.
candidates.hlni: The same total can result from different component values; an aggregate alone cannot tell you the underlying mix.
methodSteps: Show two clearly illustrative component lists with the same total.
Reveal their different components.
Ask for the breakdown before drawing a conclusion from the total.
candidates.interpretationRule: Use the breakdown to ask what differs; do not infer identical experiences from equal totals.
candidates.visibleProof: Two stacks of blocks showing different colours (subjects) but identical heights (totals).
candidates.limitations: Keep figures clearly illustrative and do not assign them to actual programmes, credits or outcomes.

demonstration.observation: The distribution of core and elective credits is different.
demonstration.nextQuestion: What does this difference imply for my elective choices?

plan.contrast: Trust_01 uses official documents to debunk title-based assumptions. Conn_01 focuses on personal task experience to empower independent inquiry. Disc_01 uses a logic puzzle to demonstrate why guessing without a source is unreliable.

issues: insight: In trust_01, the whyQuestionFollows claim that a shared title invalidates the assumption that lists are totally distinct is logically weak; shared titles can coexist with highly distinct content. Correction: Refocus the observation on how shared titles necessitate checking full programme documents to understand the actual scope of overlap, rather than assuming overlap is comprehensive.

issues: insight: In the concept conn_01, the story spine describes two friends struggling with a case study as an observation, but the mechanism relies on the student identifying their own personal needs.
